extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political philosophy; legislators and constitutional theorists seeking classical perspectives
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Aristotle's criteria and standards for constitutions, citizenship, and the legislator's role — a handbook-style treatment combining normative ideals and empirical study aimed at guiding lawgivers. Useful for readers designing or evaluating constitutions in light of classical Greek city-state assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as community for the good life
rubrics_metrics.description: The state is 'a community of well-being in families and aggregations of families for the sake of a perfect and self-sufficing life.' The city exists to achieve the highest good; its constitution should aim at making the good life possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation, institutions, and policy should be evaluated by whether they enable citizens to pursue and attain the good life. The state's purpose is not merely order or security but the facilitation of a perfect and self-sufficing life; thus lawgivers must prioritize arrangements that cultivate and sustain communal well-being rather than only instrumental functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator as expert craftsman
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator is 'a craftsman whose material is society and whose aim is the good life.' Lawgivers are experts called in to shape constitutions and public institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitution-making should be treated as technical and moral craft: the lawgiver must design institutions deliberately, using knowledge of human nature and social arrangements. The legislator's role includes shaping public opinion and moral education rather than merely administering machinery of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion and social environment as teachers of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is taught by the whole community; public opinion and social environment educate citizens, so the legislator must ensure they express the good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate schools, rituals, laws, and civic practices on their capacity to inculcate virtue. Anti-pattern: leaving moral education to 'grow up at haphazard'—legislators should proactively shape cultural and institutional norms to foster virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine idealism with empirical study
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle balances an ideal conception of the best state with careful study of actual constitutions and political experience (he studied c.158 constitutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating constitutions, weigh normative ideals against historical and empirical evidence about what works. Use comparative constitutional study to test ideals and adapt proposals to real-world constraints and patterns (causes of instability, class dynamics, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: State precedes and grounds individual parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The city (state) is a natural production and 'the whole must necessarily be prior to the parts'; man is 'naturally a political animal.' The political community is prior to the family/individual in understanding human flourishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutions by their contribution to the political whole; avoid atomistic designs that fail to consider communal bonds, civic speech, and shared justice-sentiments necessary for a functioning polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship qualifications: leisure and capacity for political reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens must be 'men of leisure, capable of rational thought upon the end of life.' Those whose lives of toil prevent political reflection (artisans, many workers) are excluded from full citizenship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating who should hold civic offices or partake in deliberation, consider whether individuals have the time and capacity for rational political judgment. Note this criterion's exclusivity: it privileges those with leisure and has implications for who is represented and enfranchised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political justice: give 'tools to those who can use them'
rubrics_metrics.description: The just distribution of political power is that which minimizes waste of political ability — power should be given to those most capable of forwarding the state's end (the good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design allocation of offices and authority to match competence and contribution to the common good. Anti-pattern: equal formal distribution without regard to capacity may produce inefficiency; conversely, absolute concentration (rule of one) risks treating citizens as mere instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed constitution principle (virtue, wealth, and numbers balanced)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed or constitutional government should balance weight given to virtue, wealth, and numbers; its stability depends on representing the actual balance of power among these interests, with the middle class as mediator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting constitutions, include mechanisms that reflect social power balances (representation of property, numbers, and merit) and strengthen a mediating middle class. Evaluate whether institutions allocate influence in line with social structure to promote stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruling and being ruled in turn as equality safeguard
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruling and being ruled by turns is an essential feature of constitutional government; equality is important to prevent rulers subordinating citizens to private ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement institutional checks (rotation, accountability, shared participation) that allow citizens to alternate between office-holding and private status, limiting permanent domination. Anti-pattern: permanent, unchecked rulers who can exploit power for private purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of revolution: class power shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Revolutions arise from changes in military or economic power among classes; democracy is often the government of the poor, oligarchy of the rich.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess constitutional designs for vulnerability to shifts in class power; include measures to mitigate concentration of military or economic resources that could destabilize regimes. Stability may be prioritized when complete ideals cannot be achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as paramount for constitutional success
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is the 'great instrument' by which the legislator ensures citizens will share the beliefs necessary to make the constitution workable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate civic education systems, public rites, and schooling for their role in cultivating shared beliefs and habits that sustain institutions. Weak civic education is a risk factor for constitutional failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator's knowledge over mere acquisition of power
rubrics_metrics.description: True statesmanship is knowledge of what ought to be done; the legislator/state-doctor is called for by the people to prescribe for an ailing constitution, not simply a politician seeking power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer appointment or empowerment of lawgivers based on expertise in constitutional design and civic virtue rather than on ambition or electoral gain-seeking. Anti-pattern: conflating the art of acquiring power with the art of governing well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of property and household management as instruments of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Household economy (property, slaves, instruments) is part of the management of the family and thus foundational to the city's functioning; slaves are described as 'animated instruments' used for household purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing social and economic institutions, consider how household organization, property rights, and labor relations support or undermine political objectives. Note ethical and political consequences of treating persons as instruments (Aristotle treats slavery as natural in this text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural hierarchy and slavery (as asserted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some beings command and others obey by nature; those 'endowed with a mind capable of reflection and forethought' are naturally superior, whereas others 'whose excellence is merely corporeal' are fit to be slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion asserts a naturalized basis for hierarchy and slavery; in evaluating historical or institutional claims, recognize this as a normative justification used to exclude groups from citizenship and rights. Analysts should note both the claim and its moral/political implications and criticisms.
